findings.title: Added test imports vitest but no dependency or runner is declared anywhere in the repo
findings.detail: src/loadConfig.test.ts imports 'vitest', yet the repository (base and branch alike) contains no package.json, lockfile, or test config declaring vitest or a test script. As committed, a fresh clone has no declared way to install or execute this test; nothing in the diff wires the new test into a runnable toolchain.

findings.title: Error types are inconsistent across the two validation paths
findings.detail: parseSettings throws TypeError for shape violations (non-object, non-string value) but a plain Error for malformed JSON, while pick throws a plain Error for a missing key. A caller trying to distinguish 'config file unusable' from an unexpected failure by catching TypeError will misclassify invalid JSON as an internal error. Behavior is intentional and encoded in the tests, so this is a taxonomy/consistency note only.

findings.title: New vitest test ships with no package.json or test config to run it
findings.detail: The diff adds src/loadConfig.test.ts, which imports from 'vitest', but the committed tree contains no package.json, lockfile, or vitest/tsconfig configuration (only README.md and src/). Nothing in the change declares vitest as a dependency or provides a test script, so the test as committed cannot be installed or executed by any consumer of this branch; the import of './loadConfig.js' also has no module/target configuration declaring the ESM/ES2022 assumptions (Object.hasOwn, Error cause) the source relies on.

findings.title: pick's missing-key error omits the config source
findings.detail: parseSettings errors include the source name (e.g. 'setting a in f.json must be a string'), but pick throws only `missing setting: a` (line 5). When Settings objects from several files are read through the same helper, the operator cannot tell which file lacks the key, unlike every parse-stage error. Not a crash — diagnosability only.

findings.title: ES2022 APIs used with no declared runtime floor
findings.detail: pick calls Object.hasOwn (line 4) and parseSettings uses new Error(msg, { cause }) (line 15); both require ES2022 / Node >= 16.9. The repo declares no engines field, package.json, or tsconfig lib target, so nothing pins a supported runtime: on an older Node every pick() call crashes with 'TypeError: Object.hasOwn is not a function' instead of the intended 'missing setting: ...' error. Cannot confirm an old runtime is actually in play, so reported as info.

findings.title: parseSettings accepts a __proto__ key
findings.detail: JSON.parse('{"__proto__":"x"}') creates an own __proto__ data property; the value is a string so validation passes and the cast on line 25 returns it inside Settings. This cannot pollute prototypes today (values must be strings, so the inherited __proto__ setter ignores them), but nothing rejects the key either, and consumers diverge: Object.assign({}, settings) silently drops the '__proto__' entry while {...settings} keeps it as an own property.

findings.title: Committed module has no consumers or file loading
findings.detail: The diff adds only src/loadConfig.ts and its vitest test; nothing else in the repo imports pick/parseSettings, and there is no file-reading, env, or wiring code — so the 'load config' branch as committed never loads anything, it is a pure string parser awaiting integration. Flagged as info because parser-only scope may be the ticket's intent.

findings.title: Added test file imports vitest but the repo declares no package.json, dependency, or test script
findings.detail: The diff adds src/loadConfig.test.ts whose first line is `import { describe, expect, it } from 'vitest'`, yet the branch contains only README.md plus the two new src files (git ls-tree -r origin/feat/load-config lists 3 files; there is no package.json, lockfile, or vitest config), and `require.resolve('vitest')` from this worktree returns MODULE_NOT_FOUND on Node v22. As committed, a fresh clone cannot execute the new tests at all — `npm test` reports a missing script and `npx vitest run` reports 'Cannot find module vitest' — so the change ships with a test suite that nobody can run from the repository.

findings.title: Undeclared ES2022 runtime requirement: Object.hasOwn and Error cause
findings.detail: pick() calls Object.hasOwn (line 4) and parseSettings throws `new Error(msg, { cause })` (line 15); both need ES2022 (Node >= 16.9, Chrome >= 93, Safari >= 15.4). The repository declares no tsconfig `lib`/`target` and no `engines` field, so that floor is nowhere guaranteed. On an older runtime the input `pick({ a: '1' }, 'a')` does not return '1' — it throws `TypeError: Object.hasOwn is not a function`, so every call fails, including for keys that are present, and the wrong error type propagates to callers expecting `missing setting: <key>`.

findings.title: A UTF-8 BOM in a settings file is reported as invalid JSON
findings.detail: parseSettings hands the text straight to JSON.parse (line 13), which does not strip a leading U+FEFF. A settings file saved by editors that emit UTF-8 with BOM decodes to `\uFEFF{...}` and fails with 'cannot read settings from <source>' even though the content is otherwise a valid object-of-strings. Stripping a leading BOM before parsing would accept such files; low impact because only some editors/OSes produce BOM.

findings.title: Malformed-JSON error message drops the parse position
findings.detail: The rethrown Error at line 15 keeps the underlying SyntaxError only in `cause`; its message is just 'cannot read settings from <source>'. Loggers that print err.message without walking err.cause lose the line/column detail, so a broken config file is hard to locate. Appending the original err.message would preserve it without losing the source name the test asserts.

findings.title: Tests omit the prototype-chain and primitive-JSON cases the code defends against
findings.detail: No test covers parseSettings on top-level primitives ('"x"', 'true', '42'), which must raise 'must be an object', nor pick on a key present only on the prototype chain (pick(Object.create({ a: '1' }), 'a') must throw 'missing setting: a') — the exact case Object.hasOwn exists for — nor that the original SyntaxError survives as `cause`. Those are the behaviors most likely to regress in a refactor since current assertions would still pass if pick were rewritten as `key in settings` with an inherited-key lookup.

findings.title: New test imports vitest and ES2022 APIs with no package.json/tsconfig declaring them
findings.detail: src/loadConfig.test.ts:1 imports from 'vitest', and src/loadConfig.ts uses ES2022-only APIs (`Object.hasOwn` at line 4, `new Error(msg, { cause: err })` at line 13). The repository (base `main` included) contains only README.md and src/ — no package.json, no tsconfig.json, no node_modules. As committed, nothing in-repo declares the vitest dependency or an ES2022 lib/target, so a fresh clone has no `npm test` script and a default `tsc` (lib below ES2022) would reject both `Object.hasOwn` and the Error options object. The logic itself is correct; the gap is that the new test file and its runtime/toolchain requirements are undeclared. Add a package.json (vitest, scripts) and a tsconfig with `lib: ["ES2022"]` (or higher) alongside the change.

findings.title: Object.hasOwn and Error cause require an ES2022 runtime that nothing declares
findings.detail: src/loadConfig.ts uses Object.hasOwn (line 4) and new Error(msg, { cause }) (line 15), but the committed tree has no package.json engines field and no tsconfig lib/target, so no runtime floor is declared. On any pre-ES2022 runtime (Node < 16.9, older browsers) Object.hasOwn is undefined and every pick() call crashes with "TypeError: Object.hasOwn is not a function" instead of returning the setting; the { cause } option is silently dropped there as well. Declare the ES2022 floor (engines/lib) or use a hasOwnProperty-based check and surface the cause message.

findings.title: Wrapped JSON error hides the parse location and cause
findings.detail: parseSettings throws new Error(`cannot read settings from ${source}`, { cause: err }) (line 15). The useful detail — the JSON.parse SyntaxError with token and offset (e.g. "Unexpected token { at position 1") — lives only on error.cause, so any caller or logger that prints err.message reports just "cannot read settings from f.json" and cannot tell what was malformed in the file. Appending the cause's message to the wrapper keeps diagnostics in the primary message.

findings.title: pick's error omits the config source name
findings.detail: parseSettings errors always name the source file ("setting a in f.json must be a string"), but pick throws only "missing setting: a" (line 5). If pick is used against settings loaded from several files, the message cannot say which file lacked the key; including source would match the convention set elsewhere in this same diff.

As committed, `npm test`/`vitest` cannot be invoked from the repo itself; the test only runs if an external harness supplies the tooling, so the suite is not reproducible from the change alone.

findings.title: Object.hasOwn and Error cause require an ES2022 runtime that nothing in the repo declares
findings.detail: pick() calls Object.hasOwn (src/loadConfig.ts:4) and parseSettings wraps errors with new Error(msg, { cause }) (line 13). Both need ES2022 (Node >= 16.9). The repo has no tsconfig.json lib/target and no package.json engines field, so nothing pins this requirement; on an older runtime the first config lookup throws `TypeError: Object.hasOwn is not a function` instead of returning the setting or a 'missing setting' error.

findings.title: formatMoney emits malformed strings for non-integer cents
findings.detail: The new module src/money.ts computes frac as String(abs % 100) with no rounding or integer guard. For float-derived cents — e.g. 19.99 * 3 * 100 = 5996.999999999999 — whole = 59 and frac = "99.99999999999999", so renderRows outputs "label: $59.99.999999999999"; input 12.5 yields "$0.12.5" and NaN yields "$NaN.NaN". Math.round(abs) (or an integer assertion) before splitting would prevent corrupted report rows. Behavior is unchanged from the function's previous location in report.ts, but this is now the shared money formatter introduced by this diff.

findings.title: formatMoney emits malformed currency for non-integer cents
findings.detail: The relocated function (moved verbatim from src/report.ts into the new src/money.ts) only handles integer inputs correctly. For input cents=99.5: whole=Math.floor(99.5/100)=0 and frac=String(99.5%100)="99.5", so the output is "$0.99.5"; for cents=-0.5 it is "-$0.0.5"; for NaN it is "$NaN.NaN". The failure walk requires a non-integer input, which the type (number) does not forbid and no guard rejects. This is pre-existing behavior carried over unchanged by the extraction, not a regression introduced by the diff, so it is rated low.

findings.title: formatMoney emits malformed output for non-integer or non-finite cents
findings.detail: src/money.ts is entirely new in this diff, and it carries over the function verbatim from report.ts: frac is computed as String(abs % 100).padStart(2, '0'), which only pads when the remainder is < 10. Input cents=1050.5 yields whole=10 and frac="50.5", producing "$10.50.5"; cents=Infinity yields "$Infinity.NaN"; cents=NaN yields "$0.NaN" (sign check is false, abs%100 is NaN). This is not a regression from the extraction — the identical logic existed in report.ts before — but the refactor is the opportunity to guard it (e.g., round to integer cents or reject non-finite input at the new module boundary).
